title: How to read a study
hook: ask who was studied, how many, and compared to what

segments.voice: Yesterday: why science belongs here. Your line was what helps. Which practice did you pick to test? Day three hundred three.

Here's a headline, made up but familiar. Study finds people who meditate are twenty percent happier. It sounds settled. It has a number. It says study. And most people read it, nod, and scroll on. But hiding behind that one sentence are three questions that decide whether it means anything at all. You don't need a lab coat or a statistics class to ask them. You need about ten seconds and a little stubbornness. Today: how to read a study.
screen: `PEOPLE WHO MEDITATE ARE HAPPIER.` → `IT HAS A NUMBER.` → `THREE QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Question one: who was studied? A huge share of psychology research has been done on university students in wealthy Western countries. In 2010 three researchers, Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan, pointed out that these people are unusual on many measures compared with humanity as a whole, and gave them a memorable nickname, WEIRD: Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic. A result from twenty-year-old psychology majors might hold for a grandmother in Lagos. Or it might not. Question two: how many? Small studies bounce around. Flip a coin ten times and getting seven heads isn't strange. Flip it a thousand times and seven hundred heads would be. A study with twenty people can find a big effect by luck; the same effect in two thousand people is much harder to fake. Question three, the one that matters most: compared to what? If people who meditate are happier, maybe meditation helped. Or maybe happier, calmer people are the ones who take up meditation. Or maybe they have more free time, or more money. That's why the strongest studies randomly assign people, one group practices and one doesn't, so the groups start out alike. And even then, ask what the other group did. Did they do nothing, or something else that also takes time and attention, like exercise or a class? Beating nothing is easy. Beating a real alternative is the real test. None of this makes you a cynic. It makes you fair. Who, how many, compared to what.
screen: `WHO WAS STUDIED?` · `HOW MANY?` · `COMPARED TO WHAT?` · `BEATING NOTHING IS EASY.` · then, large: `COMPARED TO WHAT.`

segments.voice: Take the practice you picked yesterday and turn the three questions on yourself. Who's in your study? Just you, one person. How many days have you tried it? A handful, or a season? Compared to what? Days without it, or just your hopes? No judgment. Only noticing what you'd need to know. Then let the questions rest, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
How to read a study. Three questions for any headline: who was studied, how many, and compared to what. Today's word.
screen: `HOW TO READ A STUDY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: compared to what. Check one wellness headline today with the three questions, and see how much of it survives. Day three hundred three.

howItsDone: Careful readers of health research look at the sample, its size, and whether there was a randomized comparison group, especially an active one, before trusting a headline.

options: happier, calmer people may be the ones who take up meditation.
fork.reveal: without random assignment, the arrow might point the other way; that's why the best studies randomize.

what it means: ask who was studied, how many, and compared to what.
